content: Ciprofloxacin, when administered at a dose of 2 g/day, does not produce results. However, it can increase the levels or effects of fezolinetant by inhibiting the hepatic enzyme CYP1A2 metabolism. This combination is contraindicated. Co-administration of fezolinetant with weak, moderate, or strong CYP1A2 inhibitors increases its area under the curve (AUC) and peak plasma concentration. Ciprofloxacin also increases the levels or effects of flibanserin by inhibiting the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. This combination is contraindicated, as co-administration of flibanserin with moderate or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors can lead to severe hypotension or syncope. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of alosetron by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Alosetron is associated with serious and potentially life-threatening gastrointestinal adverse effects, and its use with CYP1A2 inhibitors should generally be avoided. Aluminum hydroxide decreases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. To minimize this effect, the drugs should be separated by at least 2 hours. Ciprofloxacin and aminolevulinic acid (oral) can increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Additionally, other phototoxic drugs should not be administered with aminolevulinic acid oral for 24 hours during the perioperative period. Ciprofloxacin also increases the toxicity of aminolevulinic acid (topical) through pharmacodynamic synergism, and co-administration of photosensitizing drugs may enhance phototoxic reactions during photodynamic therapy. Ciprofloxacin and amisulpride both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If co-administration is necessary, ECG monitoring is recommended. Ciprofloxacin and anagrelide both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin decreases the effects of the BCG vaccine (live) through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination is contraindicated, as antibiotics may diminish the therapeutic effects of the BCG vaccine. Live bacterial vaccines should only be administered after completing antibiotic therapy. Ciprofloxacin and buprenorphine (in various forms, including buccal, subdermal implant, transdermal, and long-acting injection) both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Carbonyl iron decreases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. To minimize this effect, the drugs should be separated by at least 2 hours. Ciprofloxacin and ceritinib both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin decreases the effects of the cholera vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Co-administration of systemic antibiotics with the cholera vaccine should be avoided, as these agents may act against the vaccine strain. The cholera vaccine should not be administered to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. Ciprofloxacin and clarithromycin both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of clomipramine by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Concurrent use of drugs that prolong the QT interval may result in additive effects and an increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Therapy should be carefully monitored. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of clozapine by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Caution is advised when administering ciprofloxacin to patients receiving drugs that prolong the QT interval. Clozapine and ciprofloxacin both increase the QTc interval. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of cobimetinib by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If short-term use of moderate CYP3A inhibitors is unavoidable, the cobimetinib dose should be reduced to 20 mg. After discontinuation of the CYP3A inhibitor, the cobimetinib dose can be resumed at 60 mg. Ciprofloxacin and desflurane both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Didanosine decreases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Oral ciprofloxacin should not be administered simultaneously with didanosine (chewable tablets or powder for oral solution). Ciprofloxacin should be administered 2 hours before or 6 hours after didanosine. Dofetilide increases ciprofloxacin toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin and dronedarone both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. The use of dronedarone with other medications that prolong the QT interval is contraindicated. Ciprofloxacin and eliglustat both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin and encorafenib both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin and entrectinib both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin and eribulin both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin and fexinidazole both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Co-administration of fexinidazole with drugs that block potassium channels or prolong the QT interval should be avoided. Ciprofloxacin and givinostat both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If co-administration is unavoidable, ECGs should be obtained when initiating therapy, during concomitant use, and as clinically indicated. Therapy should be withheld if the QTc interval exceeds 500 ms or if there is a change from baseline greater than 60 ms. Ciprofloxacin and glasdegib both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If co-administration is unavoidable, monitor for an increased risk of QTc interval prolongation. Ciprofloxacin and hydroxychloroquine sulfate both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels of ibrutinib by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor must be used short-term (e.g., anti-infectives for ≤7 days), ibrutinib therapy should be interrupted until the strong CYP3A4 inhibitor is discontinued. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of imipramine by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Concurrent use of drugs that prolong the QT interval may result in additive effects and an increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Therapy should be carefully monitored. Ciprofloxacin and inotuzumab both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If concomitant use is unavoidable, ECGs and electrolytes should be obtained before and after initiating therapy, and periodic monitoring should be conducted as clinically indicated. Iron sucrose decreases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with multivalent cation-containing products may reduce ciprofloxacin bioavailability by 90%. Ciprofloxacin should be administered at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after using these products. Alternatives should be used if available. Ciprofloxacin and isoflurane both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin and ivosidenib both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If co-administration of a QTc-prolonging drug is unavoidable, monitor for an increased risk of QTc interval prolongation. Lasmiditan increases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin and lefamulin both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of lonafarnib by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If co-administration of lonafarnib with weak CYP3A inhibitors is unavoidable, reduce or continue lonafarnib at the starting dose. Monitor closely for arrhythmias and events such as syncope or heart palpitations, as the effect of lonafarnib on the QT interval is unknown. Ciprofloxacin and macimorelin both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Macimorelin causes an increase of approximately 11 ms in the corrected QT interval. Co-administration with drugs that prolong the QT interval should be avoided, as this could increase the risk of torsade de pointes-type ventricular tachycardia. Allow sufficient washout time of drugs known to prolong the QT interval before administering macimorelin. Mefloquine increases ciprofloxacin toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Mefloquine may enhance the QTc-prolonging effect of high-risk QTc-prolonging agents. Ciprofloxacin and methyl aminolevulinate increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Each drug may increase the photosensitizing effect of the other. Ciprofloxacin decreases the effects of oral microbiota by pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Oral microbiota contains bacterial spores, and antibacterial agents may decrease efficacy if co-administered. Complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota. Ciprofloxacin and mirtazapine both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin and olanzapine both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of olaparib by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If co-administration with moderate CYP3A inhibitors cannot be avoided, reduce the olaparib dose to 200 mg (capsule) or 150 mg (tablet) twice daily. Do not substitute tablets with capsules. Ciprofloxacin and ondansetron both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Avoid use in patients with congenital long QT syndrome. ECG monitoring is recommended with concomitant medications that prolong the QT interval, electrolyte abnormalities, congestive heart failure, or bradyarrhythmias. Ciprofloxacin and oxaliplatin both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin and panobinostat both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Panobinostat is known to significantly prolong the QT interval, and its prescribing information states that use with drugs known to prolong the QTc interval is not recommended. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of pirfenidone by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Use of strong CYP1A2 inhibitors should be discontinued before initiating pirfenidone and avoided during treatment. If strong CYP1A2 inhibitors are the only option, dosage reductions are recommended. Ciprofloxacin and pitolisant both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels of pomalidomide by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of rasagiline by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin may increase rasagiline concentration, resulting in increased adverse reactions. Patients should be closely monitored during concomitant use of these drugs. Ribociclib increases ciprofloxacin toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Selinexor and ciprofloxacin have an unspecified interaction mechanism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Patients treated with selinexor may experience neurological toxicities. Avoid taking selinexor with other medications that may cause dizziness or confusion. Ciprofloxacin and sevoflurane both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Ciprofloxacin and siponimod both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Sotorasib decreases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If use is unavoidable, refer to the prescribing information of the P-gp substrate for dosage modifications. Tepotinib increases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If concomitant use is unavoidable, reduce the P-gp substrate dosage if recommended in its approved product labeling. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of theophylline by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Concomitant use of theophylline and ciprofloxacin has decreased theophylline clearance and increased plasma levels and symptoms of toxicity. Serious and fatal reactions have included cardiac arrest, seizure, status epilepticus, and respiratory failure. If concomitant use cannot be avoided, monitor theophylline levels and adjust dosage as needed. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of tizanidine by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin and tizanidine is contraindicated. Ciprofloxacin and toremifene both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Concurrent use of toremifene with agents causing QT prolongation should be avoided. If concomitant use is required, it is recommended that toremifene be interrupted. If interruption is not possible, patients requiring therapy with a drug that prolongs QT should be closely monitored. ECGs should be obtained for high-risk patients. Ciprofloxacin and tretinoin increase each other's risk of phototoxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Both drugs have an increased risk of phototoxicity, so caution is advised with concomitant use. Ciprofloxacin and trilaciclib interact through an unspecified mechanism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Co-administration of trilaciclib (an OCT2, MATE1, and MATE-2K inhibitor) with substrates where minimal increased concentration in the kidney or blood may lead to serious or life-threatening toxicities should be avoided. Ciprofloxacin decreases the effects of the typhoid vaccine (live) through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination is contraindicated, as antibiotics may diminish the therapeutic effects of the typhoid vaccine. Live bacterial vaccines should only be administered after completing antibiotic therapy. Ciprofloxacin increases the toxicity of umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol inhaled by prolonging the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Extreme caution should be exercised when vilanterol is co-administered with drugs that prolong the QTc interval, as adrenergic agonist effects on the cardiovascular system may be potentiated. Ciprofloxacin and vandetanib increase each other's toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Co-administration with drugs known to prolong the QT interval should be avoided. If a drug known to prolong the QT interval must be used, more frequent ECG monitoring is recommended. Ciprofloxacin and vemurafenib both increase the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Concomitant use of vemurafenib with drugs that prolong the QT interval is not recommended. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of venetoclax by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If a moderate CYP3A inhibitor must be used, reduce the venetoclax dose by at least 50%. Monitor more closely for signs of venetoclax toxicities. Ciprofloxacin increases the toxicity of vilanterol/fluticasone furoate inhaled by prolonging the QTc interval. This combination should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Extreme caution should be exercised when vilanterol is co-administered with drugs that prolong the QTc interval, as adrenergic agonist effects on the cardiovascular system may be potentiated. Ciprofloxacin increases the effects of acarbose through pharmacodynamic synergism. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. Ciprofloxacin and alfuzosin both increase the QTc interval. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. Ciprofloxacin increases the toxicity of amifampridine through an unspecified mechanism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Amifampridine can cause seizures, and co-administration with drugs that lower the seizure threshold may increase this risk. Ciprofloxacin and amiodarone both increase the QTc interval. Consider administering ciprofloxacin 2 hours before or 6 hours after buffered aspirin. Buffered aspirin/citric acid/sodium bicarbonate decreases ciprofloxacin levels by reducing absorption. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. Consider administering ciprofloxacin 2 hours before or 6 hours after buffered aspirin. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of atogepant by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. Azithromycin increases ciprofloxacin toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. There is a low risk of contraceptive failure. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. Ciprofloxacin and bedaquiline both increase the QTc interval. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. ACE inhibitors may increase the arrhythmogenic potential of ciprofloxacin, possibly by increasing serum potassium levels. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels of bendamustine by decreasing its metabolism. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. Concurrent administration of a CYP1A2 inhibitor such as ciprofloxacin may increase bendamustine concentrations. Berotralstat increases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. Monitor or titrate the P-gp substrate dose if co-administered. Ciprofloxacin and betamethasone increase each other's toxicity through an unspecified mechanism. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. Co-administration of quinolone antibiotics and corticosteroids may increase the risk of tendon rupture. Consider modifying therapy, as CYP1A2 inhibitors may decrease the metabolism of 1A2 substrates. Biotin decreases ciprofloxacin levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. Administer ciprofloxacin 4 hours before or 2 hours after biotin. Bosutinib increases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of caffeine by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Caution should be used, and therapy should be monitored. The hepatic metabolism of caffeine may be decreased by ciprofloxacin, leading to increased pharmacologic effects of caffeine. Plasma levels should be monitored when used concomitantly. Ciprofloxacin and celecoxib interact through an unspecified mechanism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Ciprofloxacin increases colchicine toxicity by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Fatal drug interactions have been reported when colchicine is administered with dual inhibitors of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein. Toxicities have also been reported when colchicine is administered with inhibitors of CYP3A4. Co-administration should only occur if no other option is available. This combination is contraindicated in renal or hepatic impairment with drugs that inhibit both P-gp and CYP3A4.
